utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slightly addled brain after the election but it's Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell again, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you have something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He is present this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Oh, he is present this morning. I'm sorry, I didn't notice. Yes, could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is ushered, yesterday Ms. Korner made an objection, and I was reviewing the transcript and she is absolutely right. This was an improper question from my side, and I withdraw that question. Yeah, actually comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So noted, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Mandic, you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mandic. We have to go through yesterday's transcript to deal with a number of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 9653 [Realtime transcript read in error "963"], line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was said that in the fall of 1991 Denkovic arrived at the MUP, and I think you said Srebrenkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Srebrenikovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then page 9671, line 5 to 7. Let me remind you, my question had to do with that particular governmental session, and you said that among others in attendance, there was also Professor Simovic who was there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was deputy minster.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we also see in the transcript that Mr. Simovic, who was the deputy prime minister, was in charge of internal policy and that later on he was the chief of police and the minister of justice; is this a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may have been a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, sorry, Your Honour, can I just ask, I am not clear. What does he say was a mistake? Or your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You heard the question. Can you explain what was that slip of the tongue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Simovic was never the minister of justice and chief of police. This is obviously a mistake. However, it is in the transcript. I don't think I said that though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Korner, does this suffice by way of an explanation? In today's transcript the page number is incorrect. I said 9653. That is page 2, line 11 of today's transcript. 9653, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The next correction is on page 9681, line 25. Mr. Mandic, it is stated that members of the Special Police force who were Serbs were transferred to Vrace. In the transcript it also says that the Croats, that is to say, the Croat Special Police, those of Croatian ethnic background to Bjelave I think you said that the rest of the units, that is to say, Croats and Muslims went to Bjelavu -- to Bjelava?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the police hall in the settlement called Bjelave which is a settlement in Sarajevo. It is close to the building where the seat of the MUP is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Bjelave. The same mistake occurs on page 9690, line 23 and 9692, line 4. In the transcript we have Bjelavar and instead it should be Bjelava?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Bjelave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And one more intervention, at page 9690, line 17 something remains unclear. We discussed the meeting in Krtelji or, rather, meetings in Krtelji. If I recall your testimony correctly, concerning the first meeting in Krtelji with the members of the special unit, you went there and it was arranged there that any orders coming their way must come from the tripartite body, that is to say, from the representatives of all three ethnic communities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The second meeting at Krtelji attended by Mr. Vitomir Zepinic on orders of the minister, you said that Jusuf Pusina was there as well as and Bruno Stojic at that meeting at Krtelji where you were not in attendance, that was the second meeting in early April, that was when this Special Police Unit was divided?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the 4th of April, and I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The last intervention in the transcript, page 9695, line 17. We discussed the barricades. In line 17 it says that you were able to deal with that problem quickly because all of the party leaders were elsewhere outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina attending some meetings. Instead it should say that this is precisely why you were unable to deal with the problem; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let's go back to the 4th of April and the resignation of Mr. Zepinic. You said that he offered his resignation to Mr. Krajisnik in Krajisnik's office on the 4th of April, which is in the Presidency building of the socialist republic -- sorry, in the Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in Krajisnik's office in the Assembly building of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we heard testimony here that that meeting was attended by Mr. Karadzic, Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic, Mr. Djeric, Koljevic [as interpreted] and yourself as well as some others. Do you recall Mr. Karadzic being there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He definitely was not, and Koljevic wasn't there. Ms. Plavsic wasn't there. I think Mr. Simovic was as well as Mr. Zepinic, myself, Mico Stanisic, Mr. Krajisnik, but I don't recall any senior governmental officials as far as I recall, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to jog your memory then. We heard evidence that Dr. Koljevic was quite aggressive towards Mr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you say he wasn't even there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Koljevic is an elderly man, rather short. I don't recall Professor Koljevic being there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Mr. Karadzic was not there and that you are positive of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him being there either. I think that meeting was chaired by Dr. Simovic and Mr. Krajisnik. They hosted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We heard evidence here that Mr. Karadzic said that it was easier to replace or remove Tito than it would be with Mr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is correct, whoever said that. This is simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we also heard evidence that on that occasion several members of the special unit, Mr. Repija and Mr. Maric entered the office in full combat gear with hand-grenades, handguns, and knives?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was armed and those people did not come in at all. It was a senior police meeting and the meeting with certain members of the government at the Assembly speakers office. What hand-grenades, please? To get inside the Assembly building with hand-grenades, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We also heard evidence that in front of the office or inside it, there were some armed people in paramilitary uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paramilitary uniforms? I don't understand. What are paramilitary uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose these were not official military or police uniforms, but some rather specific uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of any paramilitary uniforms. In that building, the Assembly building, there was security at the entrance. To repeat, the meeting was only attended by Mr. Krajisnik, some governmental -- some members of the government and senior police personnel. What other people? What you are telling me is simply not true. There is a camouflage uniform and there's a regular police uniform. What is this notion of paramilitary uniform? This seems to be a brand new doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The gist of it is whether you recall anyone on the 4th of April in the Assembly building in the office or in front of it was -- whether there was anyone who was armed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In full responsibility I claim that there was no one with any weapons. All weapons were supposed to be left at the entrance. The same policy applies to all governmental and Presidency buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The last thing, Mr. Mandic. Did you know a certain Zoran who is Mr. Zepinic's driver?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him. If he was his driver, I may have known him but I can't recall him off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We heard evidence here that you asked this Zoran, Zepinic's driver, to liquidate Zepinic, that you ordered him to do this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was this allegedly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's nonsense. I'm becoming slightly irritated. Me ordering a driver to kill someone?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your answer is no, certainly. Just a few questions left, Mr. Mandic. Briefly tell me this, the Ministry of the Interior is part of state administrations, state bodies, and it is organised as such?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And as all other parts it is organised in keeping with the Law on State Administration?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that law and the law on the ministries and the law on the government. In these specific segments, these three pieces of legislation have to be completely harmonised. The regulation is rather broad in legal terms concerning any state administration bodies. It is quite voluminous as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm being reminded to ask you of another thing concerning the meeting of the 4th of April. Do you recall Mr. Stanisic threatening Mr. Zepinic that he would kill him at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me explain something about that meeting. I'm rather agitated by the questions this morning, and I don't think I understand them fully. That meeting was called, that is to say, Mr. Krajisnik summoned Mr. Zepinic and us because the joint police Special Police Unit was split up. There were words exchanged and arguments between Zepinic and Stanisic at that meeting. It was only verbal. No one wanted to kill anyone. It was rather unpleasant because Mr. Zepinic was faced with the arguments of what he had done concerning him receiving bribes, and he resigned. He was offered to stay with certain services, but he signed his resignation and left. There was no fighting, arguing, guns, or rifles. Nothing of that. These people were intellectuals. Out of the five or six of them, there were three people with PhDs there. I don't know who testified about this, but that's rubbish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. It is not my goal to agitate you whatsoever, but I do have to put these questions to you because this is the evidence we heard. Let us conclude then briefly and you can answer it with a yes or a no. You claim that at that meeting there were no serious threats issued against Mr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were definitely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before you move on to something else, could you briefly just take us through once again the positions at the meeting on the 4th of April between Zepinic and Stanisic in relation to the issue of splitting up the Special Police. What was the argument, and who took which position in this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, I can explain. I was witness to that. Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zepinic did not discuss the division of the Special Police Unit. Mr. Zepinic came to the office of President Krajisnik from another meeting where he took place in the disassociation of the special MUP unit of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That meeting was held in Krtelji which is 2 to 3 kilometres from the Assembly and government building of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Zepinic took part in that meeting and he came directly to Mr. Krajisnik's office who had summoned me, Simovic, and Stanisic before that. He called Simovic because he was deputy prime minister in charge of internal policy of the joint government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina who was also the boss to the minister of the interior and of justice in that joint government. Mr. Stanisic was there as the newly-appointed minister of the Serb police. And I was there because I was person number one from among the Serbs in the joint MUP. Veto Zepinic submitted his report on his participation in the meeting where the special unit was divided. That is when the argument ensued. All those in attendance were then informed of some of Zepinic's money, business premises, and vehicle. Some words were exchanged, and then Zepinic in his own way resigned from the position of the deputy minister in the joint MUP. And he left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I thought that the argument that took place in Mr. Krajisnik's office was an argument about the policies. So what was the matter that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The subject was the division of the special unit which had already taken place and Zepinic was reporting and informing us that he had done that together with Jusuf Pusina and Bruno Stojic. Also at that meeting facts were presented about Vito Zepinic, the things I explained a few days ago and then this verbal conflict ensued between Zepinic and Stanisic about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, what I just want to clarify is whether Mr. Zepinic and Mr. Stanisic were in agreement about the division of the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were. Zepinic, in fact, just informed us that he had already done it. And nobody among those in attendance had any argument with that. Even I agreed, but the conflict ensued when we started talking about Zepinic's -- I'm sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to clarify. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The other microphone please for Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mandic, just a few more points on this subject. I understood your evidence yesterday and the day before yesterday and also your evidence given to Ms. Korner as saying that Vitomir Zepinic, Jusuf Pusina, and Bruno Stojic had gone to Krtelji to a meeting to divide up the special unit on the orders of Alija Delimustafic then minister of the interior, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The minister had ordered that to prevent a conflict inside the special unit which consisted of people from different ethnic groups, and they were members of the special unit under arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have to repeat this for the record. Zepinic, Pusina, and Stojic went to Krtelji to a meeting in order to divide the special unit on the orders of minister Alija Delimustafic, minister of the interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a division. Members of the Serb ethnicity of the special unit went to the TEF facility, and the others were sent to Bjelave to the police hall. Delimustafic said let them split until the politicians decide how it will be organised in the future and how the future police force will be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after that meeting, Zepinic came to Krajisnik's office, and all of you were invited, and that's when he reported that the meeting in Krtelji had been finished, and that the members of the special unit were divided?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood your answer to Judge Harhoff, Zepinic was then confronted with evidence that was made public about his wrong-doings and then there was a quarrel between him and Stanisic about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question, Mr. Mandic. In your evidence in the examination-in-chief and when you were answering my questions as well, you said that Planja's house was primarily a military prison?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that military prison, by the nature of things, was guarded by the army troops?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Lieutenant-Colonel Trivunovic was commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And his units guarded the prison?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the military commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P400, page 19 in B/C/S and page 23 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were talking yesterday about the clash between Mr. Stanisic and Ms. Plavsic at the Assembly meeting of the 28th November 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conflict between them had lasted for awhile and only culminated in that Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you told us that your lawyer in Belgrade has a videotape of that Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Vujin has that videotape, and I believe Ms. Korner has it on the transcript from that session that when Mr. Stanisic said criminals have been allowed to come to Bosnia to wage war, she said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I want to read out to you, for you to confirm. Let's just find the English page. It's in front of you, it's the last paragraph on this page where Ms. Plavsic speaks. She says: "First I want say something that concerns me personally: Mico Stanisic mentioned me, and to avoid confusion and meaningless talk, mostly about the crime that is destroying our country and our people, just to make sure that you don't believe it's that kind of story, I would like to say to minister Stanisic that it is not just a rumour but it is the truth that after hearing the statement of the president of the republic, his call to all volunteers from the Serbian and orthodox countries, I sent letters to all addresses. Let me tell you, I tried to gather, to rally together all those who wanted to fight for Serbdom, so these letters were sent out. You talk about these paramilitary units and non-paramilitary units, but, excuse me, that is none of my concern. I was looking for men who wanted to fight for Serbdom, who want to fight on the territory of Republika Srpska. Those letters were sent also to the Soviet Union and they were sent out to Seselj, Arkan, and Jovic. Do whatever you like, you can accuse me on that account, but I want to make it clear that it is not a rumour. I really did that, and you condemn me if you will."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was talking about yesterday, Mr. Zecevic. The conflict arose about that because these people, these weekend warriors, were coming in and when there were no non-Serb houses available, they looted Serb houses, and Mr. Stanisic expelled them. One of those units was the Yellow Wasps in the area of Zvornik and then these people were released on -- thanks to the efforts of Biljana Plavsic. So it was like fighting windmills. It was not a conflict just between Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Stanisic, but also between me and Mr. Djeric. We were trying to point out to this member of the Presidency that it simply can't be done, you can't let paramilitary units come in and do whatever they like. And then Biljana Plavsic put a condition that she and Koljevic would stay in the Presidency if Stanisic and I stay in the government, and we were then expelled to Belgrade at the insistence of Mrs. Plavsic. It's on the record of one of the Assembly sessions and finally it suited me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clear up one thing. You will agree with me, won't you, that the reason why you and Mr. Stanisic opposed these paramilitary units was not that they had begun to attack Serbian houses as well. It was that you were in principle opposed to their conduct even when they were attacking non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were hoards of criminals who were wreaking havoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished. Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. We met about a month ago, if you remember. On behalf of the Zupljanin Defence, I'll ask you a number of questions on a limited number of topics arising from the examination-in-chief regarding my client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up P738. It's the record from that Assembly meeting where deputy Andjelko Grahovac mentioned my client. It's page 52 in Serbian in e-court and page 53 in English. Let's just wait for the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the last sentence. I will read what Mr. Grahovac said verbatim. Let's just wait for the English. There it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "I know that in the department of Mr. Zupljanin, stolen cars from Banja have been registered. I have to say that and I have information. A white Suzuki with licence plates 132 490 registered by the chief in Banja Luka, former cadres took part in that, communists amongst whom Stojan Zupljanin. I was accused of some abuse and things like that." Now, Mr. Mandic, as a professional policeman, a man who was part of those agencies were faced with accusations that you were part of the former communist system when you were trying to do your job and act against people like this Grahovac man.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And there is something behind this attack against you. I'll show you later a document that served as a reason for this attack on Zupljanin, but registration of vehicles is not done by the police -- by the centre?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan Zupljanin was head of the centre supervising 32 units which dealt with the registration of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this claim that vehicles were registered at the office of the chief, that was not true?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have prepared a set of documents I want to show you, and I have them in hard copy for you. The background of the charges against my client will be clearer from these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call document 2D030402. It's your tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's a decision from 1991. Let's just wait for it to be displayed. Mr. Mandic, do you remember an action in 1991 when Veljko Milankovic and his paramilitary unit, the Wolves from Vucjak were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision to remand him in custody signed by Stojan Zupljanin. And this decision says that this man, Veljko Milankovic was remanded in custody, and these are only some charges against him, including forgery of documents, the registration papers for the vehicles, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He was actually forging registration papers for vehicles, that was the accusation levelled against Zupljanin, right, by Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You know that this Milankovic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and then some MPs raised an outcry that Zupljanin was arresting Serbian volunteers and Serbian warrior, but finally all of us came from the former communist system. None of us originated in a democracy or capitalist ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document please be admitted into evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D73, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is tab 6. Can I please call up Exhibit 2D040154.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is an intercept of a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Andjelko Grahovac. If you look at page 2. Page 2 of this document, you can see that Grahovac was intervening with Karadzic to have these men released. The first decision was dated the 15th and then immediately on the 17th Grahovac said that these men with whom ammunition was found and Karadzic asking what does Stojan think about this, referring to Stojan Zupljanin, and Grahovac replies that those were criminals and crooks because he had received from chief Savic in Prnjavor this kind of information. And then it goes on like this. He -- Grahovac is intervening with [indiscernible] to have these men released. And if we look at page 3, Karadzic is asking him who had arrested them, and he responded that it was done by the police. There was some exchange of fire. Karadzic asked whether it was military police and the answer was no, regular police. Then Karadzic says upon whose orders, and the response is either on Zupljanin's order or this Savic from Prnjavor. So basically the whole point of this conversation is that Grahovac is asking Karadzic to intervene to have these men released?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was familiar with this event. Stojan Zupljanin consulted me about this, and I supported his idea that all those men who were involved in vehicle thefts be incarcerated and handed over to an investigating judge. And that is when Grahovac called Mr. Karadzic and asked for this intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But it didn't stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the next document, that's 2D07112. That is a tab number 7. Unfortunately, Your Honours, since Ms. Korner raised this issue later in the day, we are still waiting for translation. It's a short document. It's a telegram, and the witness can read it in its entirety pending the translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you are speeding up again. Remember the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D071112. 111 -- 2D07 -- yes, it's all right. If we can enlarge this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is a cable dated 28th November, 1991. I'm going to read it out to you. It is addressed to the command of the Banja Luka corps, attention of General Uzelac, and it was sent by Andjelko Grahovac, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is for you to read it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I want to know what he is demanding here and what threats he is make. He says here: "I demand that you urgently intervene along with Stojan Zupljanin to have Veljko Milankovic released because you have no grounds for further prosecution. I also demand that the military police return the seised camouflage winter uniforms confiscated from the fighters, 80 pieces. I also demand that Lieutenant Ratic returns 20.000 dinars, 2.000 German marks, and 2.000 Swiss francs that were confiscated from Milankovic without any receipt. Unless you do that promptly, I shall do everything I can for these and other things to be published on television and in the press." Signed by Andjelko Grahovac. So basically he is making threats, and he has demanded these things having failed to intervene with Karadzic and Zupljanin. He is sending this telegram to the army and he threatens to publicise the whole affair and that he was going to do everything in order to effect the release of this person.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, I have to show you another document in order to wrap up this topic. It's Exhibit -- just a second. 2D41, tab 8 in your binder. It's a report on criminal and other illegal activities of Veljko Milankovic and other members of the paramilitary formation from Prnjavor. It was compiled by the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka. Now, Mr. Mandic, you said that you were familiar with this affair. This is not only to do about vehicle theft. You can see, and I'm sure that you are familiar, is that there was a series of crimes committed by these groups. They intimidated people from other ethnic communities, they stopped vehicles and behaved in a very arrogant manner and which all effected the security situation in the entire region. You are familiar with the activities of this group?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, they behaved violently in the region or district of Banja Luka. This group had come from the Croatian front and started behaving violently, especially against non-Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at page 4 where it says in the second passage that months of illegal activity of this group from Prnjavor caused anxiety and fear and is causing problems among members of the police due to numerous provocations and attacks on policemen. And their activities also contributed to deteriorating of inter-ethnic tensions. And basically this is a correct assessment of chief Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the last page which is page 8. I'm going to read the last paragraph above the signature of Stojan Zupljanin. That's on page 8: "The legal measures taken against Veljko Milankovic and other members of the paramilitary formation from Prnjavor were very tendentiously portrayed and highly politicised in certain media with the obvious and well thought through intentions of raising suspicion and doubt among the members of the public, particularly among the Serbs, with regard to the legality of measures taken and eventually ending in threats to senior officers. The facts themselves presented by themselves refute any such attempt to discredit the services security organs and their personnel and show that this was not a staged arrest or a show-down with Serbian volunteers."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I'm familiar with this affair and this report was sent to me towards the end of 1991 by I think Stojan Zupljanin or his chief of the CID.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was precisely Grahovac who threatened to go to the media and smear the people who were involved in these actions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in conclusion, it is obvious what was the agenda that Grahovac had for the attacks against Zupljanin because he accused him of some problems that he was involved in?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a communist. The man was just doing his job. I received this report when I was the head of the administration for crime prevention, and as chief of the CID enjoyed my support because he carried out these operative actions. I don't know who he was among those chiefs. I think it was Jahic or a Muslim. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, since I have finished with this subject, just one more question. In your testimony, you mentioned that when you elected the judges the Muslim judges with a view to -- in view of the opposition in the Assembly, Mr. Karadzic tried to circumvent the Assembly, and he used his constitutional powers and pursuant to his decision as president of the Presidency elected and imported certain judges?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, pursuant to Article 83 of the constitution of B&H, during the state of imminent threat of war had powers to decide on certain issues instead of the Assembly. He exercised this right and on many occasions we appointed people to the post of prosecutors, judges, magistrate, people in the administration of judiciary, according to the ethnic composition of a given region.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel and the witness please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters remind you once again to slow down. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 2D021664. The English version has Exhibit number 2D021668. I suppose that's due to the fact that the translation was belated. Tab number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is one such decision taken by President Karadzic, and it refers to the courts in Banja Luka. If you look at page 2, you can see that there are judges that you mentioned. Roman numeral XII, XIII, XIV, all these were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Number XVI is Stanislav Jakl, I think he was a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then you have number XX Medic, Adem, he was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then Ruzica Topic, a Croat. Then on the last page there's Zinaida Kadic - please turn the page - she was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this basically confirms what you had been saying all the time that you were trying, actually, the president was trying to circumvent the Assembly due to this composition?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain. That took place in certain Assemblies, however, in some of the Assemblies we managed to impose our proposals reflecting the composition of all ethnicities, so it wasn't always that Dr. Karadzic used his powers in that sense. Some Assemblies did vote for the proposals of the minister of justice and regional prosecutor's offices and competent institutions that nominated people to be appointed to the Prosecutor offices and judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, concerning the election of judges in mid-May, you became the minister of justice and when you took up this position, you found a rather messy situation. Some courts were not functioning at all, and in some towns that were in the war zone, there were no judges at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no courts at all and that applied to a large number of places because the war broke out in a large area, particularly in Eastern Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these institutions didn't exist at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in some of the municipalities in Krajina such as Skender Vakuf and Teslic, Kljuc, and some other towns where there was fierce fighting at the time when you took over your duties, there were no judges at all, they had all virtually left?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the system needed time to be set up?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that to Mr. Zecevic. I think it sufficed. I told him how we worked and how we went about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in a way this also impacted the work of the police. Even when the police arrested someone, there was no one there to hand that person over to to detain that person and to have any proceedings instituted, in particular in some of the municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then there was an additional problem, as you said, which was that 95 per cent of crimes were committed by military conscripts and uniformed personnel in the Republika Srpska. The problem was how to prosecute them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the state of an imminent threat of war, all people between 16 and 65 were military conscripts, and they fell under the remit of the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the civilian Prosecutor's Offices and judiciary, they held no sway over them, they could not prosecute them, perhaps if among the perpetrators there were civilians, perhaps that link could be made and then arrest a whole group?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but they could only do an on-site investigation and then transfer the case to the military Prosecutor in question. It was all regulated by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to show you a document which will confirm what you say, which is tab 9. It is Exhibit 1D198. Your tab 9. Mr. Mandic, this is an operational work-plan created by the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka in May 1992. As an experienced policeman, you know that whenever there is a complex event involving a number of perpetrators of a crime, there needs to be a plan in order to detain the number of people concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such an operative plan can be drafted in cases of simple crimes up to terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a crime committed by these members of the SOS and Eagles as well as the Berets and TO members. There was any number of units with different names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the last page which is page 5. In the attachments we have some other events in question, but I would like to see page 5 in the Serbian for now. In e-court, I think it's page 6. The previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the English reference be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph, Mr. Mandic. It says: "As long as the Military Prosecution Office and the military court are in the process of being established, a plan cannot be implemented because most of the offenders are conscripts and members of the former TO, which is why civilian courts and prosecutors refuse to conduct these proceedings." In essence, this is what you have been saying. This confirms what you said about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to tell you that this plan indeed was implemented later on and people arrested but that's already a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I mean, it's really the objection yesterday to Mr. Krgovic. It's counsel giving evidence. I mean, occasionally the witness is asked to agree with what counsel say in evidence, but it is still counsel giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Krgovic showed an intercept, 2D04 dot, slash, whatever, 0160. Now he is clearly relying on it for the truth of the contents. He is relying on it as an accurate record. He hasn't applied to make it an exhibit presumably because the Defence are objecting to Your Honour's ruling on intercepts, but in our view, this should be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Where it was referred to in evidence, I thought that there would have been a question of it being -- whether it should be exhibited, and the questions I was going to ask is whether it had been earlier exhibited because, of course, I confess, that the list of intercepts I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. I asked the same question of Mr. Smith, and I'm told no, it's not one of the ones that we put in because it didn't directly impact on the face of it on this case. Now it does, and it clearly should be an exhibit, otherwise, as I say, Mr. Krgovic is relying on it for its accuracy and the truth of its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let me revert to Mr. Krgovic on this point, first of all. Mr. Krgovic, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are familiar with our position when the intercepts are concerned. It is our belief that for the most part such intercepts are taken out of the context, especially in the context of what Mr. Mandic was saying, and they do not meet the threshold to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you answer, could I ask the question I was about to ask, which is that you showed it to the witness, notwithstanding the basic position which we all remember the Defence takes about these intercepts. Here is a situation where you actually showed it to the witness and invited a comment on it. What was the -- what is your position as to how the Chamber should, therefore, treat this particular intercept which you are still insisting should not be admitted having yourself opened the issue on the particular intercept with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I showed two documents to the witness, and I did not seek to tender them. The first one was the cable sent by Mr. Grahovac and the second was the intercept. I just wanted the witness to be reminded of that event to provide some context to Mr. Grahovac's address in the Assembly. This is what I was striving to do. I didn't ask for either of the documents to be admitted. I just wanted to show them to the witness to see whether he can recollect the event which caused Mr. Grahovac's intervention in the Assembly. I didn't ask the witness to confirm the context or the participants in the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, I think we understand your position. Of course, you anticipate, Mr. Krgovic, that when Ms. Korner re-examines, no doubt she could return to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I need to return to this at all. It's a specious argument that Mr. Krgovic is attempting to put forward. It's rather like newspaper articles. When it suits the Defence they are perfectly prepared to use it despite their so-called objections to the authenticity, and the like, of these intercepts. Mr. Krgovic has used this intercept as evidence of the truth of what was being said and the accuracy. He cannot, therefore, escape, one, the -- as I say, the specious argument that intercepts should all be excluded and then use them; and second, if that is the purpose for which it is being used and it is accepted then the document should become an exhibit. It clearly relates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it appears to me that you are unnecessarily complicating this because the simple solution would be for you to apply in the course of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, I didn't even have to apply in re-examination. I say that it should have been ask for by the Defence, they cannot avoid it, and it should be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As Mr. Krgovic as articulated his position, no doubt he feels the need to be consistent with his general position which is perfectly understandable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it's not being consistent, Your Honour, that's the point. He may try and say that, but it's being inconsistent, and it's no different from any other document that had it been any other document we would have been asked to make this an exhibit because he says it undermines the allegation that was made by Mr. Grahovac against Mr. Zupljanin in the Assembly, and we say it's an important exhibit as well. I mean, it may not have been one we particularly chose to put in, but it should go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is that your application because in as much as the Defence hasn't sought to do so, I don't know that the Chamber can presume to make it an exhibit particularly having regard to the reasons, which, and again I use the word consistency, that the Defence has advanced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, this is the real problem. If the Defence position as maintained in their appeal or application for leave to appeal against Your Honour's decision on intercepts is that these intercepts are all in some way corrupted, inaccurate, or as was put to Mr. Mandic, that somebody in some case in BiH in the state court in Bosnia gave evidence that Mr. Munir Alibabic was in the habit of corrupting these tapes in some way, then they cannot use them. Once they are departed from that, then they are stuck with the consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We agree with everything you've said, Ms. Korner, but unless I'm missing something, why don't you simply make the application.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm quite happy. I ask in the light of the Defence's, as I say, somewhat inconsistent position, that this intercept be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I don't know that I need to call on the Defence again in response to your application. The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like just that our objection be recorded, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So noted, Mr. Zecevic. And this is a convenient point to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is being escorted back to the stand, the Registry has informed the Chamber of an error in the written reasons issued on the 26th of March for the oral decision of the 1st of March whereby the Chamber admitted into evidence intercept evidence through witness ST-108. The reasons erroneously state that Exhibit P719 in the Martic cause was tendered by the Prosecution in the present case, and that this Martic exhibit was admitted into evidence. However, this piece of evidence was not tendered by the Prosecution, and is, therefore, not admitted into evidence in this present case. In other words, Registry need not seek to assign a number to that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope you'll forgive, me, this is slightly jerky because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on. I said, I hope you'll forgive me, but I'm going in between a number of different volumes so there may be a slight pause while I do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the first matter I want to ask you about was something that was put to you by Mr. Zecevic on Wednesday the 5th, which the transcript number is, I don't know. Anyhow, he was putting to you that you were unable to speak in parliamentary debates because you were a member of the government. Do you remember, and you agreed with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what we were discussing. If there was something concerning the Ministry of Justice, something that concerned me, I was able to. As for parliamentary debates in general, I couldn't participate. What was it about specifically?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. First of all, why do you say that you couldn't participate in parliamentary debates? What was it that you said prevented you under the legislation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I was unable to participate. As far as Assembly debates are concerned on topics that do not concern the government or the Ministry of Justice, I did not participate. But when there were topics regarding justice and government work on the agenda, then I participated and even proposed topics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Mr. Mandic. It was put to you, and I'm really sorry, I marked down the original number from -- on the LiveNote of that day, and I'm still trying to find it. It's some -- yes. It came up because you were being asked -- this is, sorry -- it starts at page 9586 and continues over to 9587. Mr. Zecevic put to you: "The Assembly has its own rules including discipline measures, and these rules are written in the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly and various other regulatory provisions applying to the Assembly? "Yes. "You participated in those Assembly sessions as a member of the cabinet?" And you said "yes." And then it arose from a question I asked you: "Mr. Mandic, the Prosecution asked you why you had failed to react when you did not agree with the arguments of various MPs. Isn't it a fact that you, as a member of the government, were unable to speak at Assembly sessions even if you wished to unless a question is directed to you by MPs concerning items on the agenda that concern your ministry? Isn't it a fact that you were unable to take part in parliamentary debates?" And you said: "When the issue of the election of these judiciary officials was discussed, it is a fact that I had no right to speak. Thank you, and this particular limitation applies to all members of the government and ministers, doesn't it?" Answer: "Yes, it does." Now, I don't want to have to show you all the provisions that relate to the conduct of the Assembly and who could speak, but are you saying, Mr. Mandic, that there is a provision that prevented you on taking part in discussions in the Assembly on matters other than those that affected your ministry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is a rule that members of the executive authority may only participate in discussion of matters concerning their area of work or matters within their purview and the purview of their ministry, and that's my conviction to date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Are you able to -- I can put up the rules for you right now, Mr. Mandic, but are you able to -- from your own recollection as a long-standing minister, able to tell us under what provision you say you were prohibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I did not serve very long as minister, only eight months, and I attended only two or three Assembly sessions when there was discussion of staffing policy in the Ministry of Justice, so I did not read the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly and statutory decisions. I wasn't interested. It was not within my field of work. I was not a member of parliament or a person participating in the work of the Assembly in another capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, rather than -- because this is something that can be seen itself. Rather than going through a rather tedious exercise, the regulations governing the conduct of the Assembly are set out in the constitutional law for the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina printed in the "Official Gazette" of the Serbian people for Monday the 16th of March. And the relevant provisions one can find in Articles -- it's headed -- it's part 5, "Sessions of the Assembly."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it couldn't be that you didn't intervene because you didn't want to intervene as opposed to not being allowed to intervening?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I didn't have the right to intervene. I think it was out of place for me to speak and to start to debate with members of parliament. They elect me, not the other way around. I was not a member of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you aware of other members of the government speaking when the topics were not ones that particularly concerned their ministries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time in the government where the prime minister was Mr. Djeric, he was the one who represented and spoke for the government, but if a topic on the agenda concerned a particular ministry, then that member of the government would take the floor. And that was the general rule, people would take the floor as members of the executive authority of the government when something concerned their line of work. In my case, that was preparation of amendments concerning the Ministry of Justice proposing drafts, topics that related to the ministry, but that was always along our professional line of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's put it this way: Supposing we looked at Mr. Prstojevic's various remarks, and that is how this all arose, and effectively what he was talking about was the unlawful expulsion of non-Serbs. Do you remember we -- I don't want to go back over it, but we looked at that speech by him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that something that the minister of the interior should have intervened on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I should have added, it will be part of the law library, so I don't think I need to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm not disputing the quotation given by Ms. Korner from the document, but I believe the gist of the document, which is called the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly, is that it governs the work of the Assembly, and it's also part of the law library.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. Yes, I agree. As I say, I don't want to go through a lot of the sections because it will take a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I just want to be sure that we got the witness's answer correctly in response to your question of whether the minister of interior should have intervened on the issue of the unlawful expulsion of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He said, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because -- well, yes, but I guess the issue is if he could have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what would the witness's -- Mr. Mandic, regardless of the fact of whether Mr. Stanisic should have intervened, the issue is could he have intervened in the Assembly when the discussion was held on the expulsion of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure whether the minister of defence or the minister of police should have taken the floor, whether it should have been an MP or the president of the municipality or a member of the Presidency who was in charge of that topic of that area of work. I am not sure who should have responded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you unable to tell us under whose authority this issue fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, that would have been an issue for the army, the Ministry of Defence, but you'll have to allow that I wasn't really knowledgeable about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic, just to pick up on that, who could be more knowledgeable? You were an ex-member of the MUP having been a member of the MUP for many years, you were at the time the minister of justice, surely you are able to assist His Honour with who was responsible for dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Mr. Prstojevic and Ilidza municipality, the military commander in that area and chief of police, Tomo Kovac, were the most qualified, and when I was talking to him, I gave him certain instructions at the very beginning of the war. I don't know about later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac reported directly to Mr. Stanisic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kovac later became, in fact, minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not awhile later but a long time afterwards, three or -- two or three years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So can we move then to another matter that you were asked about, and that's this question of information and communication. At page 9589 it was put to you by Mr. Zecevic: "It's also a fact, isn't it, Mr. Mandic, that for a certain period of time until the corridor was opened, neither the government nor the ministries had almost no information about what was happening in north-west Bosnia, which is the territory of the Krajina, as well as central Bosnia, that is to say, Doboj, Brcko, and Samac; is that correct?" And you said: "Yes, I explained that all telecommunications and road communications were severed." And then I'll come on to the next bit in a moment. Now can we just examine that a little more closely, if we may. The MUP published, did it not, for the purposes of the government and the Presidency daily bulletins on what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Effectively almost from the moment that the MUP was set up, beginning of April, end of March, beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't working in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know you weren't, but this is -- just let me finish, Mr. Mandic. In fact, you were working in the MUP until the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I worked until the 24th of April until that session at Pale when the so-called Security Council informed me that I would be taking over the Ministry of Justice. From the 10th of April until the 24th. After that I started preparations for the establishment of the ministry and waited for my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have documentation on that session of that 24th of April when the decision was made that I would be minister of justice because Nikolic, the minister, failed to show up for work. And that's when I was informed. I attended that meeting, and from that moment on I started preparations for the establishment of the Ministry of Justice. The day was the 24th of April. I was exactly 14 days in the Serbian police. On the 8th, I was relieved of my duty, on the 10th I arrive at Vrace, and between the 10th until the 24th of April, I was deputy chief of the Serb -- deputy minister of police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By and large, the MUP of the Serbian republic carried on the traditions, the procedures of the old MUP of BiH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just show you some documents please for a moment, Mr. Mandic. I'm going to go back as you say you weren't there after the 24th, unfortunately I've started on the 25th, but we'll check.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please at 65 ter 939, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Serbian republic, minister of the interior, 25th of April, and it's number 6, so I hope we can assume there were five before it. We are checking to see whether we've got them. Daily report of the MUP. Can you look, please -- well, I mean, let's just go through the areas that it reports on very quickly. First of all, it talks about what is happening in Gacko. Then paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gacko.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Gacko, thank you. Paragraph 2, talks about what is happening in Prijedor, minute information about robbery. And Prijedor, of course, is in the Krajina. Sorry, perhaps you better confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go over the page in English, it's still the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two army reservists open fire in front of the Tartuf restaurant in Novi. That's also in the Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then a long report from Banja Luka. Also in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page in Serbian. Can we go to the next page in English. That's Tuzla at the bottom. Sorry, can we go to the next page in English again. Sorry, can we go back one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see reports from Bratunac, Brcko. The entire population of Brcko has left the town. Allegedly there's an agreement to divide the town. SJB Brcko remains undivided as yet, and Lukavac, whatever, and then the last page we'll see essentially goes out under Mico Stanisic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm hopefully -- and we can pull them up if necessary -- we've got all of these bulletins which start on the 19th of April, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So even before you left the MUP, Mr. Mandic, these reports were being put out. Are you saying you were unaware of them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of them. For 14 days, I was at the school at Vrace in Sarajevo while the seat of the MUP was in Pale, a neighbourhood, I can't even recall its name. And those 14 days, I stood in for Mr. Stanisic in the area of Sarajevo, I was there at the school in Vrace and I never saw these dispatches. Whether the dispatch communication was through the telecommunications of the former JNA army, I don't know, and I cannot answer that question. As for the fact that telephones and communications were not working, that is true. These are dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you can only send dispatch -- sorry, Mr. Mandic, I'm going to go on with this, but the point that you were trying to make or you leapt to agree with Mr. Zecevic, is that you weren't getting any communications at all until the corridor was opened, that neither the government nor the ministries, it was put to you, had information north-west Bosnia, which is the territory of the Krajina and central Bosnia, Doboj, Brcko, and Samac, and I'm merely trying to show you that possibly your memory is playing you tricks, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we quickly have a look, please, at the next one, P1254. 30th of April. And the information there -- and Samac was one of the particular municipalities you mentioned. According to reports in paragraph 2, received from the public security station of the Serbian Bosanski Samac, the town is now free and the situation is gradually becoming normal. Members of the Croatian paramilitary have been disarmed, some of them surrendered their weapons voluntarily. There are quite a few relatives of Alija Izetbegovic in the prison and some information about Mr. Delimustafic trying to negotiate the exchange. And I think that's all we need to know about that. And again, it's signed on behalf of Mr. Stanisic apparently. Can we go, please, to 65 ter 960. This is described as daily incident bulletin number 106. If we look at the second -- can we go to the bottom. We need to go to the next page to look at the date. It's the 22nd of May. If we go back to the first page, starts with, Sarajevo CSB, then Ilidza, and then in the area of Banja Luka CSB in Kljuc, two people were arrested. Then it goes on to other security incidents dealing with Prijedor, murders, and then over the page in English, please. Again Bosanski Novi, Banja Luka, Celinac, Gradiska, and then Bijeljina. And certainly at this stage there is Doboj and Trebinje security service centres did not submit daily incident bulletins. Can we look, please, at the 25th of -- sorry, P1266.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to note that Ms. Korner is again now she is giving evidence, and she is not posing a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I'm doing an exercise, which at the end I'm going to ask the witness whether he stands by his answer. That's all. So I'm going to have to take him through the documentation. But that will be the question. Can we -- yes. This is -- again we need to look, please, at the last page in English and the second page in B/C/S. Not a very good copy but it looks like it's the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, by that stage, you are clearly a member of the government, Mr. Mandic; is that right? As minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time-frame are we talking about, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you look, this report actually says that it's submitted to the government, the Pale staff, the office of the minister, the minister, and three under-secretaries, and it comes from the analysis and information service of the MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And while we are on that page, we can see that Bijeljina, Doboj, and Trebinje CSBs did not file their reports on security-related issues, and the telephone and other lines within Sarajevo and between Doboj and Trebinje have been down for a long period. So certainly there were problems with communications, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look then, please, at the first page in B/C/S and the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a long report from Banja Luka CSB, and, in fact, it gives this report about what was happening at the Mejdan police station. Was that an incident you were aware of, the SOS so-called Serbian defence forces attacking the Mejdan police station?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And then we see at the bottom of the English page, the explosions set off in Sanski Most by unidentified individuals caused alarm amongst town residents. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we look next, please, at 65 ter 951. Going back in time actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a daily report --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have to bring it down a bit, the English, maybe the B/C/S. Down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 19, 12th of May, 1992, and all I want to point out here, Mr. Mandic, is in the third paragraph it talks about information coming out of Bosanski Samac. 15th of May -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want now to look at the other side to show that Banja Luka was clearly receiving communications from Sarajevo or Pale. This is Mr. Zupljanin on the 15th of May, somebody I think received it on the 18th, saying we have received the communication number and date as above, from the Serbian Republic of BiH, or BH MUP, and hereby convey it in its entirety. Then on the -- I can leave that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, yes, can we look, please, at 1265. P1265. Sorry, I'm so sorry, not 65 ter, P1265.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I must -- I would just like to note one thing. We haven't been notified that any of these documents will be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is re-examination. All of these are on our 65 ter. Sorry, Your Honours, I shouldn't talk across to Mr. Zecevic. Your Honours, we notified all the documents we are going to use, this is cross-examination -- this is re-examination. As far as I know, there's no obligation to send a list in advance of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: These are documents on your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. Some of them are exhibits already. I mean, can I say, Mr. Zecevic thinks I'm taking unfair advantage, I'm simply using the documents, which are 65 ter, which have been in evidence, and, of course, he can always apply to Your Honours to re-cross examine if that's what he wants to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was just my opinion that it would be only fair that we were notified at least last night about the documents for cross-examination [sic] if they are coming from somewhere different. Those are not the documents that you used in your direct or we used in our cross-examination. That is the only thing. I mean, I just noted this, I'm not raising any problems with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could you please supplement the rules applicable in this Tribunal. I think it is the obligation of the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence the documents that they are going to use in redirect, so what is the purpose then for our giving our documents to the Prosecution for cross-examination whilst they do not do the same for redirect. I don't think it's fair and, therefore, I think you should rule that it is incumbent on the Prosecution to supply us with a list of documents that they are going to use in the redirect. Therefore, that is a prejudice to the equality of arms in these proceedings, even if it refers to 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see the logic in the position taken by Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Zecevic. However, in as much as the Tribunal in its history to date has not seen the need to formulate such a rule, I would have thought that the answer is that the ordinary rule about re-examination being based on what has arisen in cross-examination necessarily implies that any documents which implicitly fall within that -- within that box, as it were, would be allowed to be used, and for myself, I don't see the need to formulate a new rule to specifically deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour said exactly what I was going to say. It arises from cross-examination which counsel decided to pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say, Your Honours, is that this position regarding the obligation of the Prosecution was raised in the Popovic case and that there was a guide-line issued governing the acting of the parties to the proceedings. So it became the jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I continue, because I've got a lot to get through with Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. We've now got the right document. This is the daily report, and can we go in page 2 in English, I think it's maybe at the bottom of the B/C/S. We need to go to the second page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1st of June, so while the corridor operation, Mr. Mandic, is that right, are in full blast, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is the analysis and information service again sending it to the MUP, the Serbian government and handwritten delivered to the government, under-secretaries, and office of the minister, and all we need to note is that it's got a long paragraph about what is happening in Banja Luka. That's just a set of examples, but there are a number of these documents. Now in addition to SJBs reporting to the MUP, there were also, obviously, reports that the army produced. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm testifying about what I know my information was, that at the beginning of the war, the Krajina was cut off in terms of telecommunications and roads.
