In what way the police communicated amongst themselves, I know nothing about. I think that someone who worked at the police at the time should provide information about that to you. All I know is that all telecommunications and road communications were severed with Herzegovina, and Semberija, and other parts. It was very difficult to establish contacts with various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is what I know, and I'm talking only about what I know. How the police communicated is not up to me to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, sorry, can I explain. You agreed with an assertion made by Mr. Zecevic that you were not -- you, the government, were not receiving any information from the areas that you mentioned, in particular, the Krajina. I'm simply asking you whether in the light of these documents, which were clearly being sent to the government, you'd like to reconsider that answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reiterating, Ms. Korner, what I said, and that is that communications with certain parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina were cut off. We didn't have information about what was happening there. I'm talking about what was said at official meetings of the government. However, in what way the police and the army communicated is something that I cannot tell you about. I also don't know whether Mr. Djeric, the prime minister, received any information. We started receiving information from the army and the reports about events in certain areas where the Crisis Staffs started setting up camps, prisons, and things like that. That is when these commissions were set up to go into the field in order to restore the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it may be a mistake in the translation. You said, I also don't know whether Mr. Djeric, the prime minister, received any information about the army and reports about events and camps. Do you mean you do know? Because you've just said that's when these commissions were set up.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric was a member of the Supreme Command or rather, the Security Council, as a representative of the government, which included the army commander, the president of the republic, two members of the Presidency, and the minister of defence. What reports and information reach these people is something that I know nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right, you say you know nothing, but just so that we could look at one example, can we have please up exhibit -- just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P260, please. Exhibit P260.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the minutes of the fourth expanded meeting of the War Presidency, dated the 9th of June. Present, Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Plavsic, Dr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Djeric, misspelled, General Mladic, General Gvero, and Colonel Tolimir. And General Mladic briefed the Presidency in detail about the overall situation of the Serbian army and gave figures on the quantities of weapon, ammunition, spare parts, et cetera. And then under -- after a detailed discussion the following was concluded: Instruct members of the Serbian army to abide by the Geneva Conventions in their treatment of prisoners of war. So are you saying, Mr. Mandic, that after he attended this meeting, Mr. Djeric never said to anybody else in the government, there are serious problems going on with these camps and what is happening in these areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't see the connection with this document and what you have just said, Ms. Korner. I don't see in this document mentioning of any camps, any atrocities committed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Instruct members of the Serbian army to abide by the Geneva Conventions in their treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It might suggest, Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it might suggest. I agree. It might suggest anything. It might suggest that they were not informed before about the Geneva Conventions or whatever. It doesn't suggest that there was information that anything of a kind was -- I'm really just trying to keep it within the context of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right, Mr. Zecevic. Can we look, please -- can we have up 65 ter 1460, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is two days later, in fact. It's dated the 11th of June, to the Main Staff of the army. And can we have a look, please, at -- I'm not sure where it's going to be in B/C/S. One, two, three, four, fifth page in English. Yes, probably on that page, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This talks about the collection centre for the members of the paramilitary formation formed in Bileca by the order of the 2nd Operative Group Command, grew into the war in the prisoner accommodation centre operating under very difficult circumstances due to the large number of people it must accommodate, 244 of whom 16 are women and several minors. Occasional threats by pro-Chetnik forces will be attacked and liquidated along with a corps command, and we propose that persons for the centre be urgently exchanged, and the centre, if possible, relocated. Now, were these matters, matters that Mr. Djeric, when he came back from meetings of the expanded War Presidency, would discuss with other members of the government, particularly the minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this was a strictly confidential dispatch sent by the Herzegovina command to their staff. What does that have to do with the government, Mr. Djeric, or the Ministry of Justice? Look at the first page where it says strictly confidential, it's a military secret. How can a military secret be discussed in the government?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic, you said that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does that have to do with the government. I don't understand. I don't understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the part I've just read is, and what you spent sometime explaining both here and in the Krajisnik case, was this question of the exchange of prisoners. And this is what this is suggesting, isn't it, and the exchange of prisoners was a matter for the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that the army had their own commission for exchange until a central state commission was set up at the level of the government. And this is what this strictly confidential document speaks about, but since this was a military secret, I don't think that anyone from the government could have an insight into it and be informed of it. It was sent by the Herzegovina Corps to the Supreme Command, and I see this document or something like this for the first time in my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic, please understand this, all that I am dealing with at the moment is the suggestion that you agreed with it that you were not getting any information during the period of the corridor operation in particular from Krajina, Bosnia, Samac. Now, in the light of what I've just shown you, do you still want to stick to that answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you have in front of you the documents and all the minutes of the meetings of the government, what was decided and what conclusions were reached. All these documents and information presented at the government sessions were something that was acted upon, and relevant conclusions were reached. I'm saying again that regular telecommunications and road communications were severed. Whether the army, however, or the police had their own means of communications is something that I know nothing about, and I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Mandic, just concentrate, please, for a moment. It is not your position, is it -- or is it your position that no member of the government, no minister, leaving aside yourself for the moment, Mr. Stanisic, or Mr. Djeric was getting information during the course between April and the end of June, 1992 from the areas that were within the vicinity of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, Ms. Korner, about what was discussed at government session, what the agendas were. But who had what information and what kind of information, it's not up to me to guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at another matter that you agreed with Mr. Zecevic about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The obvious question to put to the witness would then be, well, Mr. Mandic, what information did you have? If you you can't tell anything about what other members of the government might have had, then what information did you receive either formally or informally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all the information that I received were presented to the government. There are minutes and conclusions and debates to that effect. And that was the only information that I could receive at the government sessions, either from the prime minister or from other ministers. And all that is contained in the documents whether in this case file or some place else. You can find the agendas, the proposals, and the conclusions. This is the information that I had. Whether someone in the government knew more or less is something that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But Judge Harhoff asked you formally or informally. You dealt with this in the Krajisnik days. Did you have informal information about camps and ill-treatment?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was focused more on Sarajevo, Ms. Korner. And I spoke about that in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll find -- I'll ask Ms. Pidwell if she can find it. You said rather more than that, but I don't want to waste time. Would Your Honours give me for one moment. Can we move, while that's being done, to what you said to Mr. Zecevic about Manjaca. He was putting to you that, in answer to questions that I was asking, you confirmed in response to my question that you had no information about Manjaca and Sanski Most. Do you remember that? And your answer was this: "Yes, that is correct. I had no information whatsoever" -- sorry, this is page 9591. "We simply couldn't obtain any information because the Krajina was completely severed. Only after the corridor had been opened, we could use the roads and telecommunications. "Q. Although your ministry had certain institutions on the ground that were under your jurisdictions, like, for example, the prison in Doboj, the district prison in Doboj, you had no contact with that institution all the way until the corridor was open; is that correct. "A. Yes. Due to this and similar problems I think that Doboj was set up only towards the end of 1992 in December after we had completed the re-organisation." First of all, can I deal with what you said about Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is part of the 92 ter package, Your Honours. At the moment it's got the number -- I think it was given exhibit numbers, but I don't know what they are. Anyhow, it's 10302.19. Tab 58. Exhibit P1318.37.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were asked about this intercept in the Krajisnik case. And by the way, while we were on the subject of intercepts, you've listened to a large number of them, haven't you, Mr. Mandic, both for the purposes of the Krajisnik case, also for this case. In any of the ones that you have listened to, have you seen any or heard any evidence that these are not your conversations as you had them with the various people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said that we knew we were being listened to by [indiscernible] and we made fun of it. He seem to have meddled with those conversations in order to create his own archives. In this conversation, you can see that I was aware of being wire-tapped. All the intercepts you presented to me as well as those that were presented to me by the Prosecution in the Krajisnik case were publicised a number of time on federal TV during the war in different versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. I agree entirely, Mr. Mandic. The only thing I'm asking you is, you've listened to these. Are these conversations, conversations that you had?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, this one, this is between you -- somebody called Ivo Rezo. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a work-mate of mine from the police. A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then between yourself and Mr. -- it should be -- is that Branko Kvesic, the ex-head of the SNB in the old BiH MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you conducted -- sorry, you and indeed Mr. Stojic and Mr. Kvesic and Mr. Rezo all remained, despite the conflict, on good terms?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war I was on good terms with all of my colleagues, whether they were Muslim or Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is the 10th of July, and the only part of the conversation I want to ask you about is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on page 11 of 23 in English. I'm going to have trouble finding it, I think, in B/C/S. Your Honours, could we try looking -- usually it's less. Could we try looking at about page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you can read English, can't you, while somebody tries to find it in the B/C/S. This is you and Mr. Kvesic talking, and you say -- or he says to you, this is the 10th of July: "There are some of our men in Manjaca, man." And he says, and you say, I'm so sorry, "in the Krajina, right?" And over the page in English, please. He says: "Yes." You say: "We can do it." "Q. What can you do about it? A lot." And then naturally -- and you say: "All right, I'll tell it to my main boss." Stopping there for a moment, who was your main boss, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prime minister Djeric and the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then Mr. Kvesic asked you to check it, please. You ask: "Where are they placed?" And he says: "You know where I am." And you say: "I know it, but where are they placed over there." You say: "They are placed somewhere on Manjaca" -- he says, sorry. And you say: "Over there in the military camp in Manjaca." So stopping there, and I'm sorry that we couldn't find it in the B/C/S, but what effectively Mr. Kvesic was asking you to do was what so many other people had asked you to do was to get somebody released, that right, or to find some of his men?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic didn't know at all ... First of all, he informed me of the existence of Manjaca and Krajina. I didn't know where it was, as you can see. And he asked me as a friend and work-mate whether something could be done so that those people would be found. He had no idea what my powers were and who was in charge of those prisons, et cetera. I asked him whether this was in the Krajina, whether Manjaca was in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what I mean, you knew in July because you say in the Krajina, right, checking that it's not him who says in the Krajina, it's you. So you knew where Manjaca was.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him if it was in the Krajina, and he confirmed this. I was completely unfamiliar with where Manjaca was let alone knowing anything about what was going on there. You can see that in this conversation. I did try to assist Branko in order to get to those people by whatever means, and this is where the conversation ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you mean it was an inspired guess when you said Krajina as opposed to anywhere else in Serbian Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the question mark, is it in the Krajina? I asked him if Manjaca was in the Krajina. You can see it in the Serbian clearly. And Branko told me it was. I had no idea where Manjaca was. You can see the question mark. And he explains that the army or rather, the TO, were in charge of that camp. I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Mandic. First of all, it's page a 7 in the B/C/S. I see it's up there. He says to you there are some of our men in Manjaca. I'm asking you how you happened to hit upon the Krajina, as opposed to, for example, I don't know, Vlasenica I heard somebody else say?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manjaca is a hill or a mountain in the Krajina, Ms. Korner. There is a large monument there to the victims of World War II. I was taught that in my history class, and I went to visit it. Manjaca is not a camp alone, it's a mountain. It is likely that the military camp was named after the mountain. It's a large mountain, and there were many civilians shot there in World War II. It's history.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying you didn't know that Manjaca was a military training-ground before this and had been opened originally in 1991 to hold prisoners from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I hear of this for the first time from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back then, please, can we go to the next page, because you say he was telling you it was a military camp. No, sorry. Where are we? The page before that. Thank you. Page before that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "You know where I am. "I know it. But where are they placed over there? "They are placed somewhere on Manjaca. "Over there in the military camp on Manjaca?" It's you, not Mr. Kvesic who calls it a camp.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have it in the Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. At the top of the page, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see the previous page where he explained to me that they were at Manjaca in the military camp, Branko Kvesic said so, and then I repeat, is it in the military camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to -- I think we've spent enough time on this, and as you are anxious to finish today and so am I, Mr. Mandic, we'll leave that. Are you still saying you didn't know about Manjaca until -- when do you say you first heard of Manjaca? When you got the report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty when I heard of it but as soon as we did ... I think once the corridor was created, Manjaca was disbanded. That was my information. It was a strictly military camp which was disbanded by presidential decree in the summer of 1992. I think my information is correct, and believe me when I say I know nothing of the camp. It was a military camp which lasted for only a short period of time as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to say whether your information is correct or not. Did you hear of a camp called Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you know that prisoners from Omarska and other places including Manjaca were transferred from there -- from Omarska and Manjaca to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, these were all military camps, military prisons. I can generalise about what I did or did not hear, but I have no official information. I didn't even know of Batkovic in Semberija. It's somewhere in the environs of Bijeljina in the barracks, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While we are dealing with that, it is your assertion that Omarska, the camp that was in Omarska was a military camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it was a police camp, was that something that the minister should have been informed of?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to get the reference in my cross-examination where this comes from, Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The cross-examination as put -- would you like to sit down, Mr. Zecevic, while I stand up. Thank you. The cross-examination adduced from Mr. Mandic or put to Mr. Mandic, that all the camps and, indeed, the majority of the prisons were run by the military. I'm now dealing with camps that he knew about that were not run by the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for the break, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just, Mr. Mandic, want to finish this question of the information that you had, and I want to remind you of what you said in Krajisnik, which you confirmed a few days ago you didn't dispute, but still dealing with information, if Mr. Zupljanin was aware that there was a camp under the control of the police for holding prisoners, would that be something that Mr. Zupljanin would be expected to report to Mr. Stanisic? And I'm drawing on your long years as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules of service, he should have. I don't know whether he did though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just quickly to remind you of what you were asked and answered in Krajisnik, this is at page 8917. It's day 5. You were asked: "What was the situation in respect of conditions and accommodation detention facilities and were guarded by or held by police," something went wrong there, I think, but anyhow, with the English recording. And your answer was: "The government, as an executive branch, was not capable to supervise directly the facilities that were safeguarded mainly by the army and to a lesser extent by the police. Various reports and information came from the ground about irregularities and inhumane treatment in these facilities and certain parts of the Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina," which is to deal with the question you were asked by ... do you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I said the same thing in the Krajisnik case and here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about here, that's why I was asking you about it. And just for the purpose of the record, you said at page 8926: "We" -- and when I -- well, the question was from Mr. Tieger: "Did the poor function of the judiciary have an impact on the issue that was concerning the government, that is, the retention of people in detention facilities and camps and the ill treatment in those facilities?" And you say: "We, and when say I say 'we,' I mean the government, we received a lot of information from the ground, negative information concerning camps, the emergence of camp, closing of camps, and the difficulty in the practice of the judiciary, and we made great efforts in order for the state commission for exchange to be equipped with [indiscernible]" and so on and so forth. And agreed, do you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said the same thing here when we were discussing the establishment of state-level commissions by the government. That was the information that gradually poured in, and we reacted to it. I think the answers were identical in both cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally on this whole topic, and I want to move to something else, the question of when Doboj was opened. Could you have a look, please, at the document which, I think was -- it's P1306. It was tab 82 in our documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I've made an error.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because I do want to finish today, so do you remember appointing Mr. Vidic in July as the warden of Doboj prison? I can show you the document, if you like, if I can find it. That's the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doboj prison was operating from June, July; is that right? Not from December, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it came into function towards the end of the year, although I'm not sure. I know that we formed one in Sarajevo first, then in Banja Luka, Foca, and Doboj next. The way we established county court is the way we followed with the prisons. I think you can all find it in the "Official Gazette". There's nothing in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Mr. Mandic, because I've made a wrong -- don't worry. The Court has seen the document, in any event. Can we now move, please, to a different topic, please. You were asked at 9627 of the transcript, yeah, about -- this was put to you: "Let us get back to Hasan Cengic and the Party of Democratic Action. You were certainly aware that in the course of 1991 the SDA party secretly sent Muslim trainees for training to the MUP of the Republika Srpska without informing the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" And I think somewhere else you talked about arming. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that the information I had was that through Hasan Cengic, the SDA, as a party, sent Muslim representatives for training to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And you were asked also about the question of the police, the Muslim police receiving arms; do you remember that? I can't lay my hand on the reference. But I want to ask you about the other side of this.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were asked about document 25. I just want to ask you about -- sorry, Mr. Mandic, could you have a look, please ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm so sorry, as I say, every now and again my noting goes completely haywire over a matter of days. Your Honours, hopefully I can come back to it at another stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, that was on the first day when you were cross-examined, you were asked and dealt with the Cutileiro plan, and you as everyone else says that the split of the MUP took place because of the Cutileiro plan, which you say was signed; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't because of the Cutileiro Plan. It was one of the reasons only because the plan foresaw the local police forces be split along ethnic lines, or to reflect the ethnic makeup of the particular region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, that's it, Mr. Mandic. You say it was one of the reasons, and certainly that's what was proposed, but you know, don't you, that it was never actually --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the basis. It is clearly stated in the dispatch that it was pursuant to the constitution of the RS, the Law on Internal Affairs, and the Cutileiro Plan, i.e., the Lisbon Agreement. You have in the dispatch all of the elements spelled out which resulted in this. It's all clear there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Mandic, you are aware, aren't you, that on the 18th of March, 1992, so well after the discussions in the Assembly, the three sides had agreed purely to a statement of principles?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the complete Cutileiro Plan and the Lisbon agreement where you clearly have provisions about the functioning of the police. It's somewhere among the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, just listen carefully to the question. I am not disputing for one moment that one of the elements of the statement of principles was that there would be a divided police force. But in actual fact, the agreement was never actually signed by anyone? It never came into the statement of principles, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that he didn't sign it. It wasn't ratified because Mr. Izetbegovic dropped the agreement upon his return to Sarajevo. When he said that he thought one thing before lunch and another after lunch, that's what he said when they asked him why he gave up on the agreement. The agreement was never ratified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it isn't, is it, Mr. Mandic, that's what I want to know, simply it wasn't a convenient, if you like, principle on which you could hang what you intended to do in any event, which was split the MUP? When I say you, I mean the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I was distracted, Mr. Mandic. Mr. Mandic, you had already - we are going to look at the February 11th meeting in a moment - you had already, hadn't you, decided long before even the statement of principles was decided, that was agreed upon, that you were going to split the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that we were going to split the MUP, but we were going to create the Serbian MUP once the problem began with the joint MUP and one of the grounds for that was the Cutileiro Plan. With the appearance of Mirsad Srebrenkovic and the relationships within the police force growing more complicated, that's how it all started. Already in February, Mico Stanisic was nominated, and we were informed that he would become the minister. And it was officialised with my dispatch, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the point, isn't it, once you had declared the Serbian Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was inevitable, wasn't it, that there would be a split in the MUP? So again, back to January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question is, Mr. Mandic, the declaration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in January, didn't that mean inevitably there would have to be a separate Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a response to the self-proclamation of one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and one at the community as independent. The Serbian people did not want to leave the common state, but once one of the nations proclaimed their independence, then we said we have to make our own state now. Our hand was forced. You know that the referendum was carried out without the participation of the Serbian people. None of the Serbs turned out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm not -- can I say straightaway, I understand your position and that of many others, but this was all caused by what happened in October. All I want to know is, is it right that once you declared the Serbian Republic a separate Serbian MUP was, as far as you were concerned, inevitable? Either yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, but just let me just explain, please, I'm your witness, let me explain this. We in the executive arm just carried out what the Assembly of the Serbian people decided. On the 23rd when the Law on Internal Affairs was published in the "Official Gazette," within eight days under that law, we created the Serbian MUP, and that's when the dispatch was sent out. It was not up to us to chart policies but to carry out the decisions of the Assembly. If the Assembly had said let's create a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina where voting will be conducted in proportion to the numbers of population, we would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine, I want to move on to the 11th of February meeting. Now, what you said about that was that it was organised by you; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you personally invited Mr. Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Mr. Delimustafic about that meeting. I had gone to see him and I told him minister, if you can come and attend yourself or send someone because we need to discuss these problems that had accumulated already, and we were going to discuss them at the headquarters of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he refused to come, that's what you are saying, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't dare to come. He didn't want to come. He would have been replaced immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he refuse to come? Did he tell you, I cannot possibly come?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said, I can't come.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no intention to have a secret meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a public building in the restaurant on the first floor of the Bosna hotel there was no intention to hold a secret meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you want to finish today, don't you? So please, please just answer the question very quietly. Right. Did you ask any of the other senior staff of BiH MUP, for example, your friend Mr. Kvesic, who was in charge of the I suppose it was then the SNB but the DRB or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... not meant to be a secret meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting to discuss the problems of the Serbian part of the MUP, 2.000 police officers who were supposed to be dismissed from the service and all other problems concerning Srebrenkovic and the operation of the Serbian MUP that did not concern the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: See, you didn't ask anybody who wasn't a Serb to this meeting, did you, other than, as you say, Mr. Alija Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why in that case, as you clearly were discussing important and, let's put it this way confidential matters, why didn't you hold it in the premises of the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more comfortable in the Bosna hotel. We had waiters there and s cafeteria nearby. It was an open room. It was not a secret meeting. A secret meeting would have been held in a closed conference room. It was just an opportunity to exchange views on a problem and to find some common ground on the problems that could not be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mandic, what you were discussing on any showing were matters really that shouldn't be known to the general public; isn't that right? These were internal police matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. We wanted the public to know about these problems, and we informed the public, Ms. Korner. We discussed it also at the headquarters of the MUP without any success. We didn't want to keep these secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so the fact that Mr. Zupljanin's deputy was a Muslim, Mr. Jahic, had nothing to do with -- that's not why you didn't hold the meeting in the CSB?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Really not. I swear to you. It had nothing to do with any intention of secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the minute-taker, Mr. Vilasovic [phoen] had been selected by you, had he, because you knew him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a driver. I can't remember what he was. He was some sort of lower-level employee. He was not an official.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You talked about him in the Krajisnik trial briefly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that name. I really don't know what position he occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the minutes ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Whether it was I who picked him or someone else, I can't even remember who chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And the final thing that I want to ask you about the actual meeting is, were the minutes sent to Mr. Delimustafic or given to him by you once they had been typed up?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took them to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You personally gave him the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Mr. Delimustafic was made aware of all of that. He knew in advance what the problem was. We presented it all to him several times. Srebrenkovic, the arrival of these police officers without vetting, the problems with official IDs. All these were well known problems in the functioning of the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Delimustafic do anything about, go and talk to anybody about what was clearly being discussed as a split in the MUP on the 11th of February?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you didn't ask Mr. Zepinic to this meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because Mr. Zepinic, as you knew, was, in fact, totally against the idea of splitting up the MUP, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what his views were. I can't speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you were asked to look again at the dispatch that you sent out immediately after that, which is -- it was Defence document tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that dispatch by heart.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. I just want to have it up again for a moment. P527. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were asked about it and said it was a public and open dispatch and you had -- and it was received by those on duty in the respective police stations and centres. Now, you agree, it's -- it doesn't set out what the conclusions were, or indeed, what the meeting was about. You simply say: "Following the conclusions reached at the meeting held in Banja Luka, please set up and have a meeting with all senior executives." So anybody reading that wouldn't have the faintest idea of what had been discussed, would they, on the 11th of February?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you interpret this. It says: "Following the conclusions" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop. Does that tell anybody who might read this open dispatch what the meeting was about or what the conclusions reached were? Simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, I wasn't focused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's fairly obvious. Right, you sent it to Zupljanin, Banja Luka CSB, a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to all those police officials who attending the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but this is what I want to know. You say it was an open meeting and you were sending it to everybody. Why didn't you send it to the Bihac CSB?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that man would not have forwarded it to all the police agencies on the ground. I asked these people to inform all the agencies in their territory, including, of course, Muslims and Croats, because I said in the area the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP because some of these parts interfered -- sort of were involved in our problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't send it to the Livno CSB, and there were Serbs working there as well, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the majority were Croats, these problems discussed at the meeting were not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Didn't go to Tuzla or Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not send it to areas where the leaders were Muslims who advocated the unlawful expansion of the MUP. That's Bihac, Zenica, Tuzla, these three centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you said at one point to Mr. Zepinic, after a long explanation at page 9676 when you were talking about the Cutileiro Plan and all the rest of it, and you explained that now the Dayton Accords effectively implemented the Cutileiro Plan, and you said: "And what did we have in the meantime? A bloody war for four years, and who is responsible for that, I ask you?" Now, could you have a look, please, at one of the documents that was part of the 92 ter package. And it is, I don't know what the exhibit number is, but it was 1489 on the 65 ter list. P739. Thank you. I'm sure you remember this, Mr. Mandic. This was an interview conducted with you in a magazine called "Ekstra." It's not clear, I don't think it was ever discovered when it was published. And you were asked, page 2 in English, and it's on that page, the whole thing is one page: "How did you personally take the political conflict and severance of relations between the Republika Srpska and the FRY, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? As a man I'm very devoted to both Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic. With Karadzic and Krajisnik, I began the war in Sarajevo and now when I'm sitting here and watching what happened, I find justification for the Serbian leadership of Yugoslavia. I justify it by the fact there was an objective threat of putting twelve million people in total isolation, which would have disastrous consequences, and in order to avoid that, Slobodan Milosevic and his associates had to do what they did, in my opinion." And then further on you were asked this, you were dealing with people who had left, and it said -- sorry, next page, please, in English. Karadzic's family is at Pale, as is the family of Momo Krajisnik. And then the question, it says: "Biljana Plavsic is not the only person who got her relatives out. Many delegates have sent their families to Belgrade and places in Yugoslavia." And you said: "As for state leadership, Karadzic's family is at Pale, as is the family of Krajisnik. Koljevic's at Belgrade, as is Biljana's family. We differed in respect to this issue Mico Stanisic and I started the war in Bosnia. We separated the Serbian part of the MUP and set out to Vrace. We were supposed to be shot." And then you go on talking. Can we go to the next page in English. He's talking about Ostojic a swindler. Stanisic was dismissed from office. "The fact that some see me as Slobodan's man is a result of the fact that Mico Stanisic and I are friends. Mico Stanisic and I started the war in Bosnia." That's what you said, wasn't it, then Mr. Mandic, some time ago now, looking at the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't know what this newspaper is, but this interview was given probably several years after the fact, for propaganda purposes during the conflict between me and Biljana Plavsic. I was telling the truth here, whereas this interview is unauthorised. It's not true, and it has nothing to do with what actually happened in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Mandic, that what you said -- first of all, do you agree that's what you said, leaving aside whether it's true or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never in my life. I never said I started the war in Bosnia. That's nonsense. I'm not the kind of man who would have said something like that. I have rather a high opinion of myself, but still, I would not have been able to overestimate my role to such a degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you saw this article when it came out, did you ask them to print a retraction?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw this article was when it was given to me -- shown to me by Mr. Tieger when I was interviewed as a suspect. I don't even know in which city this newspaper is published. And it's obvious that this was in the 1990s, after the war, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure it was after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look now please at the interview, the one that you gave to "Slobodna Bosna" on the 10th of April 1998 which is 1389 -- 65 ter 1389. Sorry. P735. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now before we go into this, do you agree that you gave this interview to "Slobodna Bosna?"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just show me the date and the year? I can't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you can see the date if we enlarge the B/C/S. It's 10th of April, 1998. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were shown that in the Krajisnik case. This is part of your ... so did you give that interview?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1998 is a long time ago now, but when you saw it in the Krajisnik case, did you remember it? Or before the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably presented there. I don't recall if I was able to to recall it at that trial or not. This was 12 or more years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just look at what you apparently said there. It's headlined: "It wasn't just Serbs and Croats negotiating, we've offered the place of the president to the Yugoslav government to Izetbegovic too." And then this is said to be a quote from you, "there would be no war if Ramiz Delalic was arrested in time. Dragan Kijac, Mico Stanisic, and myself organised the barricades in March. Now you have been telling the Court that this was a spontaneous outbreak. Did you say that -- first of all, did you say that to this magazine?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really don't remember. 1998, some Sarajevo newspaper. And how could I talk about Mr. Izetbegovic as the prime minister of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just move on in the English to the fourth page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The March barricades -- was the question: "The March barricades in Sarajevo were organised by the SDS. Did you take part in their organisation, and what did the SDS want to achieve with them?" And then you dealt with the bridegrooms, the killing of the Serb wedding. And you said: "Quite a few municipal leaders from the SDS demanded that something be done in protest since they knew the perpetrator had been identified but not arrested. Had Delalic then been arrested, even if he stayed in prison for just ten days, tensions would have calmed down. Then the people on their initiative took out to the streets and erected barricades. In order to avoid chaos and as a sign of our Serbian strength, Rajko Djukic headed the committee for the organisation of barricades. I do not wish to hide anything, Dragan Kijac, Mico Stanisic, myself, and some others from the MUP took part in this, and we organised everything so as to avoid blood shed and show the public and Izetbegovic that they could not act like that." Now, was that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, this is what I said in this trial, we organised and supervised the check-points in order to avoid bloodshed. It was not us who erected the barricades. What it says here is that the municipal leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party took to the streets on their own initiative. Not only I, Stanisic, and the rest controlled these people, as did everybody in the Ministry of the Interior. We wanted to stop the bloodshed. Of course you couldn't expect the Muslim police officers to go to the barricades and try to calm the tensions and the people, and not a single incident happened within the span of 48 hours thanks to the Serbian part of the police in the joint MUP. We didn't organise the barricades. I and the other Serbs instead took care that no incidents took place in the MUP. Whereas, the ordinary people took to the streets on their own initiative. This is what you read. Although I don't remember every detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Rajko Djukic headed the committee for the organisation of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, since the political leadership of the SDS was abroad. The remaining representatives of the people in Bosnia, Rajko Djukic, and Muhamed Cengic, the vice-prime minister, organised this and tried to overcome the situation in a calm way, and in that they were held by the Serbian police officers. As I said, you can't expect Muslim police officers to go to the barricades. That would result in bloodshed. It was not us who organised the barricades. We took care and we made effort to avoid bloodshed, and this is what I said before this Trial Chamber. It is true that Muhamed Cengic and the vice-prime minister and Rajko Djukic negotiated about the ways of overcoming the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the same interview, you dealt with, didn't you, what had happened at the school at Vraca? We can show it to you, if you like, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary, just ask me a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what you saw -- what you said there about this was that there was mistrust within the special unit, a difference of opinion between the special unit members of Serbian nationality and the others. You then discussed the split of the building. "That's what we agreed on. I invited Karisik and 35 special unit members on Saturday, the 5th of April to enter the building. They had barricaded the school, arrested my brother, along with two or three men. 170 men had come to Croatia for a training course. We knew about it, but we decided to go to the school -- into the school nevertheless. If the members" -- over the page, please. "If the unit had not gone in, we would have been driven out of Sarajevo. We would have lost both legality and legitimacy?" It was for that matter, wasn't it, Mr. Mandic, one of the matters that you stood trial at the state court, of which charge you were acquitted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Vraca, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it was -- I think I'll leave it at that. Thank you very much. Now, I've nearly completed what I want to ask you about, Mr. Mandic, but you say that the paramilitaries, and you've been shown the speech made by Plavsic, were entirely the fault, really, of Biljana Plavsic for bringing in Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't think it was her fault solely. But it was her who invited these paramilitary formations to come over, and she said at the Assembly meeting that she had sent a letter to various addresses to Serb patriots inviting them including Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, who was a leader of the White Eagles, and I don't know which other paramilitary formation, to come over whilst Mico Stanisic put them to prison. There were Yellow Wasps and others, and she felt offended by that. That was a conflict between the chief of police and a member of the Presidency, and it culminated at this Assembly session. And, you know, just one sentence more and then you can proceed. You know what Biljana Plavsic said and I quote, that: "It will take 6 million Serbs to die for another 6 million of Serbs to live in freedom."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've said that before. Did Biljana Plavsic ever accuse you and Mico Stanisic of involvement or knowledge of a man called Batko who was operating in the Grabovica area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you read her book?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wouldn't do that. Let me tell you, Ms. Korner, Biljana Plavsic accused me of a variety of things. Some that were appropriate and some that were completely inappropriate, and she did this not only to me but to other people that she disliked for various reasons, and all those things were untrue, and I don't have any intention of reading the book written by Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there was never an incident where she came in, you two were with Dr. Karadzic, you and Mr. Stanisic, and she accused you of allowing a paramilitary called Batko to commit killings in Sarajevo in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were just talking about her bringing in the major -- the paramilitary formations and about Stanisic putting them into prison. If she did that, that would make us her opponents. She cannot accuse us of the same thing that she did. She should make up her mind. I don't know what you are talking exactly. You are talking about some paramilitary formations. This woman was very personal, but I don't want to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm not going to discuss it further, given your answer, Mr. Mandic. I just want to ask you this: You talked about the Yellow Wasps. Did you ever attend a meeting in Sekovici, which is I think in Zvornik municipality, together with Mico Stanisic where the paramilitaries who were in Zvornik came up for discussion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. Sekovici is a separate municipality. It's not part of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. It's next to Zvornik then, is it, or near Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, between Vlasenica and Zvornik. I don't know, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know somebody called Jovo Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo Mijatovic, no, I don't recall. And who was he, what was his position? Can you please help me refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you say you don't know him, then -- I think he was the SJB in Zvornik. Ring any bells with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Spasovic was chief of police in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't recall Mr. Jovo Mijatovic being --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just - I'm correcting myself on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In any event, the point that I want to make is this: Were you ever before you moved on to be minister of justice at any meetings where the problems in Zvornik of the paramilitaries were raised with you and Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember ever being in Zvornik to attend a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware at any stage from any information you received from Mr. Stanisic or anyone else that arms were being given to members of the Yellow Wasps by the SJB in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period are we talking about, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. On what basis? On what grounds?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just asking if Mr. Stanisic ever said to you that there was a report that the Yellow Wasps had been supplied with arms by the SJB?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I correct myself. Mr. Mijatovic was the head of the SDS, not the SJB chief. Does that ring any bells with you now?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that man at all. I don't know who he is. That was 18 years ago. Whether he was an MP or was he simply the mayor. He probably must have been someone totally unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, finally, Mr. Mandic, on this, you talked about -- at length about Mr. Zepinic and the manner of his resignation and who was there. And you say that his resignation had nothing to do with his opposition to the split in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took part in this meeting when the special unit was divided. That's what Zepinic told me. He was part of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So as far as you say, he agreed to this? He agreed to the division?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time he was an unfortunate man who didn't know what to do. We all knew what he had done, and on the other hand, he couldn't do anything out of his own volition. He didn't have his own will at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Mandic, concentrate on the question. Is it your assertion, I just want to make sure we all understand this, that he agreed to the division of the special unit and of the MUP generally?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that he agreed to the division of the special unit and that he voluntarily accepted to be the first minister of the police in December 1991 and member of the Security Council. If he didn't agree with that, why didn't he resign in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, please, I'm asking you, you told us you were present at this meeting. Please, first, is it your contention, it is your evidence, as you said to Mr. Zecevic and others, that he agreed to the split in the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he went there in order to split it pursuant to an order of Delimustafic, the minister of police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And he did not oppose the split in the MUP, is that what you are saying, please, Mr. Mandic? Yes or no. It's is a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he wasn't opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what went on the argument at the meeting before he put his resignation letter in had nothing to do with the split of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to do only with Vitomir Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, I want you, if you would be kind enough to watch this time so there's no discussion about what you may or may not have said, part of an interview that you gave to television in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the number of that is 1318.15. And it's part of the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we stop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have the indication of where this part begins, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it starts at 036.40 in the transcript in English at page 6. I think we need to go back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There were great interruptions of relations among people. You know, we are, and I consider myself like that too, children of the system, who were learning about the brotherhood and unity and life together since we were seven years old. I must say that at the time, special unit was used to carry out searches in Serbian villages, Serbian houses, Serbian settlements. I remember well, they were in Pofalici, in that house from here, to search for weapons. They also went to Bileca and Gacko, and that provoked great negative reaction by all of us, officials of Serbian nationality in MUP, as well as Serbian people. I couldn't watch anymore that my Karisik, and other members of Special Forces go and search Serbian houses. We demanded ... we insisted several times ... there was one meeting that Jusuf Pusina, Bruno Stojic and me, participated in. It lasted for six hours and we had it with members of special unit. I must say that Drazen Vikic, commander of special unit, for whom I must say he is a very correct person, expert and professional ... he even demanded that there is an order, signed by three parties, in order to put special unit in movement. That means the right of veto, meaning consensus that, if the special unit is sent somewhere, it can't do anything without the agreement of all three officials of the three nationalities. That was Bruno Stojic at that moment, Jusuf Pusina and me, as the chiefs of administration. I remember well that, after that big, tiring meeting, Jusuf Pusina told me: 'There's nowhere to go ... Mandic, you succeeded in dividing the MUP, there is no more unified MUP.' Because, that was in fact the way it was. If Jusuf Pusina, as the head of police, I mean that department, can't put special unit in motion, meaning Delimustafic, that means that unified MUP doesn't exist anymore. And somehow, we carried it out. Unfortunately, however, Vito Zepinic, meaning Alija Delimustafic, used all methods and lobbying people, called on our best special unit members, Miodrag Repija, Maric, and Jevtic, I believe, those are our best men, and promised them apartments, this and that, and it came to slight dilemma in the psychic of those people. You know, it is very hard to leave the system of one country. But, at that moment, Milenko Karisik played a very important role, because he notified me, the presidents Krajisnik and Karadzic, and with the great wisdom of Krajisnik, we called Vito back to the Presidency, I mean, Assembly. We took the special unit out, Karisik took them to Blazuj, and it came to significant division of special unit, and it is often that after the division of special unit everything else divides too."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, how much time do you need? I have a few questions to put to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- the transcript is in anyhow. Your Honour, I can stop now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, what you said there, in fact, is not what you told the Court, is it? It was clear, wasn't it, that there was no agreement and you were being accused of being responsible for the split in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, what you heard me say now is the truth. This is the confirmation that a three-party meeting took place and -- that a tripartite meeting took place and the executives talked about the special unit. I did somehow attribute in this interview more importance to myself than was due credit to me, but the fact is that the special unit was separated based on a political decision, and this is what I spoke about in this interview and that was also confirmed in my trial by Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But what you say here -- leave aside your trial and what may or may not have been said by Mr. Delimustafic for whatever reason, but what you say here was, isn't it clearly, is that Mr. Zepinic was opposed to all of this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. This was an interview, and I tried to over-emphasise my role. That is what I wanted to do, to over-emphasise my role in the whole affair. What I'm telling you today is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the same interview, and we haven't got time to play it, you gave also yourself a full account of what happened at Vraca, didn't you? Which can be seen further on in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a version to be presented to the press and to the public. That is how I thought at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say it was a version, do you mean you weren't telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these were my thoughts about everything that was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I realise that you must be confused and tired by being pulled around, but I hope you can maintain your concentration for another seven minutes before we adjourn. I have three small questions to you. The first is in relation to the intercept that Mr. Krgovic showed to you where you spoke with Branko Kvesic, and about you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I showed it to him, Your Honours. Mr. Krgovic showed him the Grahovac one, I showed him the Kvesic one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise. Ms. Korner showed you that intercept. And what struck me when I was reading through it, was the fact that here you have Kvesic asking you for assistance to help out a few Serbs who, for some reason, had been maintained in Manjaca; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Branko Kvesic was in Mostar, and I was the only one whom he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But my question would be, if these camps were under the jurisdiction of the army, why wouldn't he call the minister of defence, and why did you agree to help him out rather than just referring him to the competent authority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic worked in the police alongside with me, and I was the only one he knew among the people he believed could help him. Of course, I didn't refuse my friend this help that he was looking for. Of course I went to inquire about these people. It is only natural the minister of defence didn't know who he was and he would be reluctant to communicate with him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. My next question to you relates to the information that you gave us a couple of days ago, I think, now, about the jurisdiction of the military courts as opposed to the jurisdiction of the civilian courts over crimes committed in the Republika Srpska in the summer of 1992. And the evidence you gave was that the military courts had total jurisdiction over all of these camps and indeed over all of the offences that could somehow be related to the conflict. You also said that in that same period because of the fact that the military court had taken over virtually everything, the civilian courts had very little to do. I think you told us that in one of the municipalities, only two cases were heard in eight months by the civilian courts. My question to you now in relation to this information is.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How long did that situation last really, because I think we have evidence, either by yourself, I can't remember, or by someone else, to suggest that at a certain point some of the jurisdiction was handed back to the civilian court in order to help out the situation of an overloaded military judiciary, while the civilian judiciary had nothing to do, so at one point there was a transfer of cases or another distribution of the crimes that were heard by the courts. So, first of all, is it correct that at some point the many cases or some of the cases were transferred from the military courts to the civilian courts, and secondly, when did that happen, if it happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the jurisdiction of the military court was never transferred to the civilian courts. Although, only a month after my appointment to the ministerial position, first in June, then in August, I asked for that to happen. However, the ultimate refusal to transfer jurisdiction from the military courts to the civilian courts happened at the Assembly meeting when General Gver o said that that would be unconstitutional. And in September I resigned as the minister of justice and one of the reasons was precisely that, meaning that the civilian judiciary was unable to perform its duties, whereas the military judiciary didn't do their job. So the army never allowed any transfer of competencies from the military judiciary to the civilian one, although, I insisted on it a number of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question relates to the scenarios that you had described throughout your testimony here before us. Namely, that there was disagreement between the Presidency and at least some members of the government about how to deal with the war crimes and crimes against humanity. I'm particularly here referring to the crimes that were committed in the camps. I'm referring to these camps because at several other trials before this Tribunal, the fact has been established that crimes were consistently committed throughout 1992, and this Chamber has taken judicial notice of those -- of the facts that those crimes were committed in the camps. So my question to you now is, what you considered to do at the time when you were given information that these things happened, you took measures to try and stop them, and these measures failed. What did you think yourself actually about whether or not you wanted to be a part of this? I realised you resigned as a minister in September, but did you discuss this with the others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the summer of 1992 we began receiving information from the field about the camps and inhumane treatment inside those camps concerning civilian non-Serb population. I testified here before saying that there were commissions formed immediately on the request of the government which toured throughout Republika Srpska in an attempt to ascertain what was indeed happening. And they proposed measures in that regard. Those measures were forwarded to the Supreme Command of the army, to the Presidency, to the Assembly speaker, and the prime minister. I think those documents make part of this case file as well. The Ministry of Justice as a civilian body we could only propose measures. In a state of an imminent threat of war, one could not meddle with the competencies of the army, which I assert, was the sole body responsible for the camps where non-Serbs were detained, whether civilians or military conscripts and able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What was the -- I realise we have to stop now, so maybe I should just leave it at that then. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic, for your attendance over the past week and your assistance to this Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home, and more especially, we trust that there's no repeat of the unfortunate incident that affected your travel to the Tribunal. We now take the adjournment until 9.00 on Monday morning in this courtroom where we are scheduled to reconvene. I wish everyone a safe weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.
